mcqs.question: In Meeting Rooms I, after sorting meetings by start time, why is it sufficient to compare only adjacent pairs instead of every pair of meetings?
options: Because sorting removes all overlaps between meetings automatically
Because only meetings that were adjacent in the original unsorted list can overlap
Because if meeting i doesn't overlap meeting i-1, it cannot overlap any earlier meeting either, since starts are non-decreasing after sorting
Because Meeting Rooms I only needs to check the first and last meeting in the sorted order
mcqs.explanation: Once sorted by start time, if meeting i starts at or after meeting i-1 ends, it also starts at or after every meeting before i-1, since those end even earlier. That monotonicity is what collapses an O(n²) all-pairs check into a single adjacent-pair pass. Sorting doesn't remove overlaps — it just makes them detectable in one linear scan.

mcqs.question: Why might you choose the min-heap-of-end-times approach over the two-sorted-arrays sweep for Meeting Rooms II?
options: It has a better asymptotic complexity, O(n) instead of O(n log n)
It avoids sorting the meetings entirely
It naturally extends to assigning specific room identities to meetings, not just counting how many rooms are needed
It works correctly even when a meeting's end time is earlier than its start time
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches cost O(n log n) overall, so complexity isn't the deciding factor. The heap's advantage is that popping a stale end time and pushing a new one identifies an actual free room you can assign a meeting to, whereas the two-array sweep only ever produces a count of how many rooms are needed, never which one.

mcqs.question: In the two-pointer sweep for Meeting Rooms II, why does the comparison use strict `starts[s] < ends[e]` rather than `starts[s] <= ends[e]`?
options: Using `<=` would change the algorithm's complexity from O(n log n) to O(n)
Strict `<` is only needed when meetings have zero duration
Using `<=` would fail to detect any overlapping meetings at all
With `<=`, a meeting starting exactly when another ends would be counted as simultaneously active, inflating the room count by one
mcqs.explanation: A meeting ending at 10:00 has vacated the room by the time a meeting starting at 10:00 begins, so they shouldn't both count toward concurrency. Strict `<` processes the tied end before the tied start, freeing the room first. Swapping to `<=` would double-count that instant on every back-to-back scheduling pair — common in real calendars.

mcqs.question: A database connection pool needs to be sized for a batch of queries whose start times and durations are all known in advance. Which technique directly gives the minimum pool size needed so no query ever waits?
options: Sort the queries by duration and take the median duration as the pool size
Divide the total number of queries by their average duration
Apply the greedy earliest-finish-time algorithm used for Erase Overlap Intervals
Compute peak concurrency via the same start/end event sweep used for Meeting Rooms II
mcqs.explanation: Minimum pool size is exactly the peak number of simultaneously active claims on a shared, interchangeable resource — the same computation as minimum meeting rooms, solved by sweeping start/end events and tracking the running maximum. Erase Overlap Intervals solves a different question (minimum removals), not resource sizing.

mcqs.question: What is the overall time complexity of both Meeting Rooms I and Meeting Rooms II, and what dominates it?
options: O(n log n), dominated by the sort — the adjacent-pair check or the sweep itself is only O(n)
O(n), since both algorithms only need a single pass through the input
O(n²), because every meeting must be compared against every other meeting
O(log n), since binary search is used to locate each meeting's room
mcqs.explanation: Both variants sort first (or build a heap, which is equivalent in cost) and then do a single linear scan or sweep. The sort is the more expensive part at O(n log n), so it sets the overall bound even though the scan itself is O(n).
